answer_text:
The surface \(S\) is the parabolic cap \(z = x^2 + y^2\) with \(0 \le z \le 1\), which corresponds to \(x^2 + y^2 \le 1\). (If the phrase “above \(z=1\)” is interpreted literally, the surface is unbounded; however, the flux over any radially truncated portion also vanishes by symmetry, so the answer remains \(0\).)

Parametrize \(S\) using cylindrical coordinates:
\[
x = r\cos\theta,\quad y = r\sin\theta,\quad z = r^2,
\]
with \(0 \le r \le 1\) and \(0 \le \theta \le 2\pi\). The position vector is
\[
\mathbf{X}(r,\theta) = \langle r\cos\theta,\, r\sin\theta,\, r^2 \rangle.
\]
Compute the upward-oriented vector area element:
\[
\mathbf{X}_r = \langle \cos\theta,\, \sin\theta,\, 2r \rangle,\quad
\mathbf{X}_\theta = \langle -r\sin\theta,\, r\cos\theta,\, 0 \rangle,
\]
\[
\mathbf{X}_r \times \mathbf{X}_\theta =
\begin{vmatrix}
\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\
\cos\theta & \sin\theta & 2r \\
-r\sin\theta & r\cos\theta & 0
\end{vmatrix}
= \langle -2r^2\cos\theta,\, -2r^2\sin\theta,\, r \rangle.
\]
The \(z\)-component is positive, so this gives the upward orientation.

Evaluate the vector field on \(S\):
\[
\vec{F} = \langle y,\, x,\, zy \rangle
= \langle r\sin\theta,\, r\cos\theta,\, r^2 \cdot r\sin\theta \rangle
= \langle r\sin\theta,\, r\cos\theta,\, r^3\sin\theta \rangle.
\]
Then
\[
\vec{F} \cdot (\mathbf{X}_r \times \mathbf{X}_\theta)
= (r\sin\theta)(-2r^2\cos\theta) + (r\cos\theta)(-2r^2\sin\theta) + (r^3\sin\theta)(r)
= -4r^3\sin\theta\cos\theta + r^4\sin\theta.
\]
The surface integral becomes
\[
\iint_S \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{S}
= \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^1 \left( -4r^3\sin\theta\cos\theta + r^4\sin\theta \right) dr\, d\theta.
\]
Integrate with respect to \(\theta\):
\[
\int_0^{2\pi} \sin\theta \, d\theta = 0,
\qquad
\int_0^{2\pi} \sin\theta\cos\theta \, d\theta = 0.
\]
Therefore, the entire integral is \(0\).

\[
\boxed{0}
\]
